title: Hard to be born human (179–182)
hookLine: hard is it to be born human, hard the life of mortals, hard to hear the true teaching

lines: THE PRICE TAG ON A DAY.
cards: It's a Tuesday. You woke up, found the coffee, checked the weather, and went through the usual list of complaints. And yet: you woke up.
You have a mind that can wonder about its own life. You're hearing words first spoken twenty-five centuries ago that still reached you. None of that feels rare, because it happens every day.
One verse in chapter fourteen turns this ordinary Tuesday over to show the price tag.

teach.b: The chapter opens by praising the Awakened One as trackless: no desire can lead him anywhere, so there's no trail to follow him by. Verse one eighty-one says the gods envy those who are awake.

Then verse one eighty-two, in Max Müller's words: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals, difficult is the hearing of the True Law, difficult is the birth of the Awakened."
In Pali, each line begins with the same word, kiccha: hard, difficult, rare. Hard to be born human. Hard to live as a mortal.
Hard to hear the true teaching. Hard for a Buddha to appear at all. Four rarities stacked up, and you're standing on all four.
In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture of how rare. Imagine a yoke with a single hole, tossed on the ocean and blown about by the winds.

teach.h: A BLIND TURTLE AND A YOKE.
teach.b: Once every hundred years, a blind turtle rises to the surface. What are the chances it puts its head through that hole?
That, he says, is how rare it is for a being who has fallen into the lower realms to come back to a human birth. You don't have to hold the Buddhist view of many lives to feel what this verse does.
It takes the thing you complain about every morning and shows you it's a winning ticket.
Buddhists hear it as urgency, not guilt: this life, with a mind that can learn and a teaching within reach, is the rare chance. The list of complaints can stay; it just doesn't get the whole day.

how: Many Buddhist traditions, Theravada and Tibetan alike, begin practice by reflecting on the preciousness and rarity of a human life, often using the Buddha's image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

o: a duty owed to the Buddha

p: a blind turtle and a yoke
the Buddha, led by no desire
even the gods envy the awake

s: human birth, a mortal life, hearing the true teaching, and a Buddha arising.
the turtle rises to the surface once a year
once every hundred years, and the yoke has only one hole.
Buddhists hear this verse mainly as a reason for guilt
they hear urgency: a rare chance, not a debt.

games.q: a blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years. a yoke with one hole drifts on the whole ocean. what is the Buddha comparing it to?
o: the chance of being born human.
the chance of meeting a friend.
games.why: that's how rare the tradition says a human birth is: so rare that an ordinary Tuesday is a winning ticket.

practice: Go through this ordinary day slowly: you're breathing, rare; you can hear, rare; someone, somewhere, you love or who loves you, rare; food, a roof, a moment to sit, not everyone has these; a teaching you're thinking about, rare.
Don't force gratitude; just let each ordinary thing be seen once, the way you'd look again at something you almost threw away. Then rest in this one rare breath.

wordCard.voice: Kiccha. Hard, difficult, rare: verse one eighty-two says rare is human birth, rare a mortal life, rare the hearing of the teaching, rare the arising of a Buddha.

orig.note: Pali: a human being — in verse 182, gaining a human birth is kiccha, hard.

carryVoice: Your line: this life is rare. Even on a Tuesday. Day one hundred ninety-three, done.
